doc-43.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid When Choosing a MetaTrader Grey Label Provider

blocks.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid When Choosing a MetaTrader Grey Label Provider

Switching grey label providers is possible, but it’s never pleasant. You’re moving client accounts, trade history, configurations and integrations, usually while trying to keep the brokerage running as if nothing is happening. Most brokers who go through it say the same thing afterwards: we should have asked more questions at the start.
This piece is about those questions. Below are the metatrader grey label mistakes we see most often, and what to do differently.
Mistake 1: Choosing on Price Alone
It’s understandable. Launch budgets are tight, and when one provider quotes noticeably lower than the others, it’s tempting to stop looking.

The trouble is that headline prices hide a lot. A low setup fee might come with volume charges that rise sharply as you grow. A cheap monthly fee might leave out the backup server, extra manager terminals or plugin support. Some providers make their margin on add-ons you only find out about once you’re committed.
What to do instead: ask every provider for an estimated total cost at launch, after twelve months and at your target volume. Compare those totals, not the opening quote.
Mistake 2: Not Checking Who Holds the License
Your grey label runs under someone else’s MetaQuotes license. If that license is shaky, so is your brokerage.

Some providers are resellers of resellers, several steps removed from the actual license holder. That’s not always a problem, but it adds risk and often slows down support, because every serious issue has to go up the chain.
Ask directly who holds the master license, how long they’ve held it, and what your position is if anything changes. If the answer is vague, treat that as your answer.
Mistake 3: Assuming “Admin Access” Means Full Control
Most grey label providers advertise admin access. Not all of them mean the same thing by it.
Some lock certain settings. Others restrict which plugins you can install, or insist all changes go through their team. You may only find out when you try to configure something and it’s greyed out.
Before you sign, ask for a written list of anything you won’t be able to change yourself. Better still, ask for a test login to the admin terminal and look around.
Mistake 4: Ignoring What Happens If You Leave
Nobody likes planning for a breakup at the start of a relationship. But this one matters.
Find out:
Whether you’ll get a full export of client data and trade history
In what format, and how quickly
Whether there are exit fees or long notice periods
What happens to your server name and branding
A provider confident in their service won’t make leaving difficult. One that dodges these questions probably relies on lock-in to keep clients.
Mistake 5: Underestimating Support Needs
On a quiet Tuesday afternoon, support barely matters. On a Sunday night before the market opens, with your server not responding, it’s the only thing that matters.

Many brokers accept “24/7 support” at face value. In practice, that can mean a ticketing system someone checks the next morning. Ask what live monitoring is in place, what the response times are for critical issues, and whether those times are in the contract.
Then test it. Send a few technical questions during the sales process, including one late at night or on a weekend, and see what comes back.
Mistake 6: Overlooking Integration Experience

Your MetaTrader server has to work with your bridge, CRM, payment gateways, risk tools and reporting. If the provider hasn’t connected those particular tools before, you’re paying for their learning curve.

When you choose metatrader grey label provider partners, ask which bridges, CRMs and liquidity providers they’ve already integrated on live servers. Ask for examples, not just a general “we support everything”. Real experience means fewer surprises in your first weeks.
Mistake 7: Picking Server Location Without Thinking
Server location affects execution. If your server is on one continent and your liquidity provider on another, every order carries extra latency. Traders notice, especially scalpers and EA users.
Some providers offer one location and don’t mention it unless asked. Make sure you know where your server will be, whether you can choose, and how close it is to your main liquidity source.
Mistake 8: Skipping Reference Checks
Sales calls show you the best version of a provider. Other brokers show you the real one.

Ask for two or three current clients you can speak to, ideally ones similar in size to your brokerage. Ask about their worst outage, how quickly it was fixed, whether fees have changed since they joined, and whether they’d sign again.
If a provider won’t give you any references, that tells you something.
Mistake 9: Rushing the Decision
Providers sometimes push a deadline: a discount ending Friday, limited server slots, a promotion for new brokers. Occasionally that’s genuine. More often it’s meant to stop you comparing.
Your grey label will likely sit at the centre of your brokerage for years. An extra week of checking won’t hurt your launch. A rushed choice might hurt everything after it.
Mistake 10: Not Thinking About Growth

What works for 200 clients may not hold up at 5,000. Before signing, ask how the provider handles growth. Can your server be upgraded easily? Will pricing change sharply at higher volumes? Can you add more servers, more plugins or new platforms later?
Choosing for where you’ll be in two years saves you a migration in eighteen months.
A Simple Checklist Before You Sign
Total cost estimated at three stages of growth
Master license holder confirmed and checked
Written list of any admin restrictions
Clear exit terms and data export process
Support response times written into the contract
Proof of integration with your chosen tools
Server location agreed
At least two reference calls completed
If a provider passes all eight, you’re in good shape.
Conclusion
Most metatrader grey label mistakes come from taking things on trust that should have been checked. None of these checks take long, and each one protects you from a much bigger problem later.

doc-44.title: How Much Capital Do You Need to Start With MetaTrader Grey Label?

blocks.text: How Much Capital Do You Need to Start With MetaTrader Grey Label?

It’s usually the first question new brokers ask, and the most frustrating to answer, because the honest reply is “it depends”. But it doesn’t depend on mystery. It depends on a handful of decisions you can make up front: where you’re regulated, how you plan to execute trades, and how quickly you want to grow.
Once those are clear, working out your forex broker startup capital becomes far more manageable. Here’s how to break it down.
The Grey Label Itself Is Rarely the Biggest Cost
This surprises a lot of people. They expect the platform to eat most of the budget, then discover it’s often one of the smaller line items.

A grey label costs a fraction of a full MetaQuotes license, which is a big part of its appeal. You’ll usually pay a one-time setup fee and then a monthly fee for the server, license and maintenance. Some providers also charge by number of accounts or trading volume.

Prices vary a lot between providers, so get written quotes from a few. When you build your metatrader grey label budget, plan for at least twelve months of platform fees, not just the setup cost. Running out of money in month six because you only budgeted for launch is a very common way for new brokerages to fail.
Regulation Is Usually Where the Big Money Goes
Your regulatory route drives your total capital needs more than anything else.
Minimum Capital Requirements

Every regulator sets a minimum amount of capital your company must hold. These range from relatively modest sums in some offshore jurisdictions to hundreds of thousands of euros or more with stricter European and tier-one regulators. The figure often depends on the type of license too. A broker that holds client positions on its own book is usually required to hold more than one that only passes orders through.
This money isn’t spent, but it is locked up. You can’t use it for marketing or salaries.
Setup and Ongoing Compliance

On top of the capital itself, there are legal fees, application fees, local office or director requirements, audits, compliance officers and annual renewal costs. In stricter jurisdictions, these can easily outweigh the platform costs several times over.
Talk to a specialist lawyer before you settle your budget. The jurisdiction you pick will reshape every other number in your plan.
Technology Beyond the Platform
A grey label gives you the trading server. You’ll still need to pay for the rest of your stack.
Liquidity bridge: connects your server to liquidity providers, usually with a setup and monthly fee
Forex CRM and client portal: handles onboarding, KYC, deposits and withdrawals
Risk management tools: essential if you run any B-book flow
Website and hosting: your brand’s front door
Back office and reporting tools: especially if your regulator expects detailed reporting
Some grey label providers bundle a few of these together, which can save money and integration headaches. Check the cost of each piece individually so you know what you’re really paying for.
Liquidity and Execution Costs

If you’re running A-book, many liquidity providers ask for a deposit or margin before they’ll give you access. The amount depends on the provider and your expected volume, but it’s money you need to set aside before launch.

If you plan to run B-book or hybrid, you’ll need enough capital to absorb client wins. A few lucky traders in your first month can make a serious dent if your balance sheet is thin. This is one of the most overlooked parts of startup capital, and one of the most dangerous.
Payment Processing

Payment processors that work with forex often ask for a rolling reserve, holding back a share of deposits for a set period as protection against chargebacks. Some also want an upfront security deposit.
That means part of your clients’ deposits won’t reach your operating account straight away. Plan your cash flow around it.
Team and Operations
Even a lean brokerage needs people. At minimum, you’ll usually need:
A compliance officer, often a regulatory requirement
Someone to manage the dealing desk and risk
Customer support covering trading hours
Back office staff for payments and account queries
Sales or account managers, if you’re working with direct clients
Some of this can be outsourced at first, but salaries and contractor fees add up quickly. Budget at least a year of running costs here.
Marketing: The Cost People Underestimate
You can have a perfect setup and no clients. Marketing in forex is competitive and expensive, and many ad platforms restrict financial services advertising, which pushes costs up further.

Common channels include IB and affiliate partnerships, content marketing and SEO, paid ads where permitted, events and expos, and social media. IB programmes are often the most cost-effective at the start, because you pay mainly on results.
Whatever channels you choose, give marketing a real budget. Brokers who pour everything into setup and leave nothing for growth rarely get past their first year.
Putting a Budget Together
Rather than chasing one magic number, build your budget in layers:
Regulatory capital: the amount your chosen jurisdiction requires you to hold
Setup costs: licensing, legal, grey label setup, integrations, website
Twelve months of running costs: platform fees, tech subscriptions, staff, office, compliance
Liquidity and risk buffer: deposits for liquidity providers, plus a cushion for B-book exposure
Marketing: a realistic first-year budget for bringing in clients
Contingency: an extra margin for delays and surprises, because there will be some
Add those together and you have a figure grounded in your actual plans rather than a guess.
Ways to Keep Initial Capital Lower
If the total looks daunting, there are sensible ways to reduce it:
Start in a jurisdiction with lower capital requirements and expand later
Launch with a smaller set of instruments and account types
Choose a provider that bundles the server, CRM and bridge
Rely on IB partnerships instead of heavy paid marketing at first
Outsource compliance, support or dealing until volume justifies hiring
What you shouldn’t cut is your risk buffer or your runway. Those are what keep you alive while you build.
Conclusion

Your forex broker startup capital depends mostly on regulation, execution model and growth plans. The grey label is an important piece, but usually not the heaviest. Build your metatrader grey label budget around a full year of operations, keep a healthy buffer, and you’ll give your brokerage a real chance to grow.

doc-45.title: Introducing Broker (IB) Programs for MetaTrader Grey Label Businesses

blocks.text: Introducing Broker (IB) Programs for MetaTrader Grey Label Businesses

Ask any established broker where their best clients came from, and there’s a good chance the answer is a person, not an ad. A trading educator with a loyal following. A local partner who runs workshops. A money manager who brought their investors along. That’s the introducing broker model, and for many brokerages it does more for growth than any paid campaign.

If you run a MetaTrader grey label, you’re in a good position to build a strong forex ib program, because you control the server, the account groups and the data that make IB rewards work. Here’s how to do it well.
What an IB Actually Does

An introducing broker refers clients to your brokerage in exchange for a share of the revenue those clients generate. They don’t hold client funds or execute trades. That stays with you. Their job is to find traders, build trust and point them your way.
IBs come in many shapes:
Trading educators and course creators
Signal providers and analysts
Local agents who handle relationships in a specific country
Affiliates who run websites, YouTube channels or social accounts
Money managers bringing their investor base
Each brings a different kind of client, and each tends to want a slightly different deal.
Why Grey Label Makes IB Programmes Easier to Run

On a white label, your IB options are often limited by how the host sets up groups and reporting. With a grey label, you have admin access to your own server, so you can design your programme around your business instead of someone else’s setup.
A well-built metatrader grey label ib structure lets you:
Create dedicated account groups for each IB, with their own spreads or commissions
Track every trade back to the IB who referred the client
Pull accurate volume and revenue data straight from your own server
Adjust conditions for top-performing partners without affecting other clients
That flexibility matters. Good IBs compare brokers carefully, and the ability to offer tailored terms is often what wins them over.
Common IB Reward Structures
There’s no single right way to pay IBs. Most brokers use one of these models, or a mix.
Rebates per Lot
The IB earns a fixed amount for every lot their clients trade. It’s simple and transparent, and it’s popular with IBs whose clients trade actively.
Spread Markups

The IB’s clients trade on slightly wider spreads, and the IB keeps the difference. This gives the IB some control over their earnings, but it needs careful handling so clients still get competitive pricing.
Revenue Share

The IB receives a percentage of the net revenue their clients generate. This lines up the IB’s interests with yours, but it requires clear, trustworthy reporting, because IBs will want to see exactly how revenue is worked out.
CPA (Cost per Acquisition)
A one-off payment for each client who meets set conditions, such as a minimum deposit and trading volume. This is more common with affiliates than traditional IBs, and it needs strong fraud controls.
Multi-Level Structures
IBs can recruit sub-IBs and earn a share of their commissions. This can grow your network quickly, but it gets complicated fast. Keep the number of levels manageable and the rules very clear.
The Tools You Need
Running an IB programme on spreadsheets works for about three partners. After that, it becomes a source of errors and arguments.
At minimum, you’ll want:
An IB module in your CRM that tracks referrals, works out commissions and handles multiple levels
Real-time sync with your MetaTrader server so trade data feeds into commission calculations automatically
An IB portal where partners can see their clients, volumes and earnings without emailing your team
Tracking links and promo materials that make it easy for IBs to send traffic your way
Automated payouts on a fixed schedule
The IB portal especially is worth getting right. Partners who can see their numbers clearly trust you more and complain less.
Pay Accurately, Pay on Time

This sounds obvious, but it’s where many IB programmes fall apart. IBs talk to each other. A broker who pays late or gets calculations wrong will hear about it, and so will every other IB in that network.

Set a clear payout schedule and stick to it. Make sure commission calculations match what IBs see in their portal. If a mistake happens, fix it fast and explain what went wrong. Your reputation with partners is worth far more than the cost of a correction.
Protect Yourself From Abuse
Most IBs are honest, but any reward system attracts a few people looking to game it. Common problems include:
IBs trading heavily on their own linked accounts just to generate rebates
Clients and IBs coordinating trades that cancel each other out across accounts
Fake or duplicate accounts set up to trigger CPA payments
Churning, where clients are pushed to overtrade to boost commissions

With a grey label, you can watch for these patterns directly on your server. Risk tools that flag linked accounts and unusual trading behaviour are worth having before your programme grows. Clear terms that allow you to hold or cancel payouts for abuse help too.
Treat IBs as Partners, Not Lead Sources
The brokers with the strongest IB networks don’t just send a contract and a tracking link. They invest in the relationship.

That might mean a dedicated account manager for top partners, co-branded webinars or materials, early access to new account types or features, or regular calls to hear what their clients are asking for. IBs are close to the market. They often know what traders want before your marketing team does.
Getting Started
If you’re building a programme from scratch, keep the first version simple:
One or two reward structures you can explain in a sentence
A clean IB portal with accurate, real-time data
A fixed monthly or weekly payout schedule
Clear terms covering abuse and payout conditions
Add complexity only once the basics run smoothly and you understand which partners are actually bringing in quality clients.
Conclusion

A strong forex ib program can become your most dependable growth channel, as long as it’s built on accurate data, fair rewards and on-time payouts. Running a metatrader grey label ib setup gives you the control to design the programme your partners actually want, rather than whatever a host allows.
If you’re planning to launch or improve an IB programme, MetaGreyLabel can help you set up the groups, tracking and integrations to support it.

doc-46.title: White Label, Grey Label or Turnkey? Choosing the Right Model

blocks.text: White Label, Grey Label or Turnkey? Choosing the Right Model

Spend a little time researching how to start a brokerage and you’ll run into three terms over and over: white label, grey label and turnkey. They’re often presented as three options on the same menu. They aren’t, quite. White label and grey label describe how you access the trading platform. Turnkey describes how much of the whole business comes ready-made.
Once you see it that way, the choice gets much easier. Here’s how the three fit together, and how to work out which one suits your plans.
White Label: Renting a Branded Space

A white label puts your brand on a MetaTrader server that someone else runs. You share that server with other brokers, and the host controls the core configuration. You get a manager terminal, branded client terminals and the ability to open accounts and manage clients.

It’s the quickest and cheapest way to get a platform running. The trade-off is limited control over liquidity, execution settings, plugins and data. For brokers testing a market or working with a very tight budget, that trade-off is often worth it.
Grey Label: Your Own Server, Someone Else’s License

A grey label gives you a dedicated MetaTrader server running under your provider’s master license. You get admin access, so you configure groups, symbols, swaps and execution yourself. You pick your liquidity providers, add the plugins you want, and your client data sits on your own server.

It costs more than a white label and needs more technical know-how to run, but it gives you far more freedom. Many brokers move to a grey label once they’ve outgrown a white label, while others start there because they already have the experience and client base to use the extra control.
Turnkey: The Whole Business in One Package

A turnkey forex broker solution is about scope rather than platform access. Instead of buying the trading server alone and sourcing everything else separately, you get most of what you need to launch from one provider.
A typical turnkey package might include:
The trading platform, on either a white label or grey label basis
A forex CRM and branded client portal
Liquidity access and a bridge
Payment gateway integrations
Risk management and back office tools
Website design and development
Help with company formation and licensing
Ongoing technical support
The idea is simple: one contract, one point of contact and one integrated stack, rather than six vendors who have never worked together.
How They Combine
Here’s where people get confused. Turnkey isn’t a third type of platform. It’s a package that sits on top of one.

So you might come across a white label turnkey solution, which is fast and inexpensive with limited control. Or you might choose a metatrader grey label turnkey setup, where you get your own server with admin access plus the CRM, bridge, payments and website already connected around it.
The second option is popular with brokers who want real control over their trading environment but don’t want to spend months stitching together tools from different suppliers.
Weighing Up the Options
If Speed and Low Cost Come First

A white label, possibly as part of a basic turnkey bundle, gets you live fastest with the smallest upfront spend. It’s a reasonable way to test demand, learn the business and build an initial client base.
Just go in knowing you’ll probably outgrow it, and check how easy it is to move on later.
If Control Matters Most

A grey label gives you control over execution, liquidity and configuration. If you have an experienced team and clear views on how you want to run your book, sourcing each component yourself lets you pick the best tool for every job.
That said, it takes time and technical effort, and you become the one responsible for making everything talk to everything else.
If You Want Control Without the Assembly

A grey label turnkey package is the middle path. You keep the server control that makes a grey label worthwhile, while your provider handles integration and delivers a working brokerage instead of a box of parts.

For many first-time brokers with a solid budget, this is the most practical route. It’s also common among established businesses expanding into forex from related fields, such as crypto exchanges or financial education companies, who know their audience but not brokerage technology.
Questions That Point You the Right Way
Answering these honestly usually settles the choice:
How much capital do you have for setup and your first year of running costs?
Does your team include people who have run a MetaTrader server before?
Do you already have liquidity relationships, or do you need introductions?
How quickly do you need to launch?
Do you already own any parts of the stack, like a CRM or website, that you want to keep?
How much control do you need over execution and risk from day one?

If you’re short on time, technical staff and existing tools, turnkey makes sense. If you have strong opinions and an experienced team, assembling your own stack around a grey label may suit you better.
What to Watch For With Turnkey Packages
Turnkey solutions can be excellent, but they come with their own risks:
Lock-in: if everything comes from one provider, leaving can be harder. Check whether you can swap out individual components later.
Hidden weak spots: a package might include an excellent platform but a mediocre CRM. Assess each part, not just the overall bundle.
Vague licensing help: “assistance with licensing” can mean anything from a full application service to a list of law firms. Ask exactly what’s included.
Bundled pricing: ask for a breakdown so you can see what each part really costs.
There’s No Permanent Choice

Plenty of brokers start on one model and switch later. A white label turnkey can become a grey label as the business grows. A grey label turnkey can be gradually unbundled as you bring parts of the stack in-house. What matters is choosing something that fits where you are now, with a clear route to where you want to be.
Conclusion

White label and grey label decide how much control you have over your trading server. Turnkey decides how much of the rest of the business arrives ready to go. A turnkey forex broker setup built on a grey label gives many brokers the best of both: real control and a much faster, simpler launch.

doc-47.title: Trader's Room and Client Portal Features in a MetaTrader Grey Label Setup

blocks.text: Trader’s Room and Client Portal Features in a MetaTrader Grey Label Setup

Your traders spend most of their time in MetaTrader. But almost everything else they do with your brokerage happens somewhere else: signing up, verifying their identity, funding an account, moving money between accounts, asking for help, withdrawing profits. All of that happens in the client portal, often called the trader’s room.

It’s easy to treat the portal as an afterthought, something you sort out once the server is running. That’s a mistake. For many clients, the portal is your brokerage. It’s the first thing they use and the place they come back to every time money is involved.
Here’s what a strong forex client portal should include, and how it fits into a grey label setup.
Why the Portal Matters So Much

Think about it from the trader’s side. They’ve probably used a few brokers before. They know what a smooth sign-up feels like, and what it feels like to wait three days for a withdrawal with no updates.

A good portal makes your brokerage feel organised and trustworthy. A clumsy one makes even excellent execution look suspect. Traders reasonably assume that if the basics are messy, the rest might be too.
With a grey label, you run your own MetaTrader server, so your portal can connect to it directly. That makes it possible to build a far smoother experience than many white label setups allow.
Registration and Onboarding
The first few minutes count most. Good trader’s room software keeps registration short and gets clients to a funded account as quickly as your compliance rules allow.
Features to Look For
A short sign-up form, with extra details collected later rather than all at once
Social or email sign-up options where your regulator allows them
Mobile-friendly design, since many clients sign up from their phones
Clear progress steps so clients know what’s left to do
Language options for the markets you serve
KYC and Verification

Clients should be able to upload ID and proof of address straight from their phone camera. Automated checks can approve straightforward cases quickly and send unclear ones to your compliance team. The portal should also show clients exactly where their verification stands, so they aren’t left guessing or emailing support.
Account Management
Once verified, traders want control over their own accounts without having to contact anyone.
A good portal lets them:
Open new live or demo accounts instantly
Choose from the account types you offer, such as standard, raw spread or swap-free
Change leverage within the limits you’ve set
Reset MetaTrader passwords
See all their accounts, balances and equity in one place
Because a grey label gives you admin control over your server, these actions can sync to MetaTrader immediately. A new account opened in the portal is ready to trade within moments.
Deposits, Withdrawals and Transfers
This is where the portal earns its keep, and where most complaints start if things go wrong.
Deposits

Offer the payment methods your target markets actually use: cards, bank transfer, local e-wallets, and crypto where permitted. Deposits should show up in the client’s MetaTrader balance automatically once payment is confirmed. Every extra step between paying and seeing funds is a chance for a client to lose patience.
Withdrawals

Clients should be able to request a withdrawal in a few clicks, see its status clearly, and get notified at each stage. On your side, the back office should flag requests that need extra checks while letting routine ones go through quickly.
Internal Transfers
Traders with multiple accounts often want to move funds between them. Instant internal transfers are a small feature that clients really appreciate.
Trading Insights and Reports
Many traders like to see their performance outside MetaTrader. A portal can show:
Trade history and account statements
Profit and loss over custom periods
Deposit and withdrawal history
Downloadable reports for tax or personal records

Some brokers go further with simple analytics, such as win rates, average trade duration or most-traded instruments. It’s not essential, but it’s the kind of detail that makes a portal feel thoughtful.
Support and Communication
The portal is a natural home for support. Look for:
A ticket system where clients can follow their requests
Live chat linked to the client’s account details, so agents don’t have to ask for login numbers
A notification centre for important updates, such as margin warnings, new account types or scheduled maintenance
An FAQ or help section covering the questions your team gets asked again and again
Good support tools cut your workload too. Clients who can find answers themselves raise fewer tickets.
Features That Add Extra Value
Once the essentials are solid, extra features can set your portal apart.
Copy Trading and PAMM Access

If you offer copy trading or managed accounts, the portal is where clients browse strategy providers, check performance and choose who to follow. Investors should be able to see their allocations and results without logging into separate systems.
IB and Affiliate Areas
Introducing brokers need their own section to see their referred clients, trading volumes and commissions. A clear, accurate IB area helps you attract and keep good partners.
Education and Market Content
Some brokers put tutorials, market analysis, economic calendars or webinar sign-ups in the portal. It keeps clients coming back and gives newer traders a reason to stay with you as they learn.
What Your Team Needs Behind the Scenes
The client side gets the attention, but the back office matters just as much. Your team should be able to:
View a client’s full profile, accounts and trading activity in one place
Approve KYC, deposits and withdrawals with a clear audit trail
Move clients between groups or change conditions when needed
Pull reports for compliance and management
Set permissions so each team member only sees what they need
When your forex client portal and back office share data properly with your grey label server, your team spends less time chasing information and more time helping clients.
Choosing the Right Software
When comparing trader’s room software, a few questions sort the strong options from the weak:
Does it integrate directly with your MetaTrader grey label server in real time?
Can it be fully branded, including domain, colours and emails?
How well does it work on mobile?
Which payment providers does it already support?
Can it grow with you to cover copy trading, PAMM and IB programmes?
How are updates and new features handled?
Ask for a live demo connected to a test server. Go through it as a new client would, from sign-up to first withdrawal. You’ll spot problems that no feature list will tell you about.
Conclusion

Your trading server does the heavy lifting, but your client portal shapes how traders feel about your brokerage. Get registration, payments and account management right, and everything else becomes easier.
If you’re planning the client side of your grey label setup, MetaGreyLabel can help you choose and connect a portal that fits your markets and your traders.

doc-48.title: Compliance and KYC Basics for MetaTrader Grey Label Brokerages

blocks.text: Compliance and KYC Basics for MetaTrader Grey Label Brokerages

Compliance rarely makes it into the exciting part of a brokerage launch. Nobody gets into forex because they love writing AML policies. But it’s the part that decides whether you keep your license, keep your bank accounts and keep your payment processors. Get it wrong and it doesn’t matter how good your platform is.

A grey label gives you a lot of control over your trading environment. That control comes with responsibility. Here are the basics every grey label brokerage should have in place, and how your technology can make the job easier.
First, Know Where the Responsibility Sits

Your grey label provider runs the MetaTrader server under their master license. But they’re not your compliance department. Your regulatory obligations belong to your brokerage, the licensed entity dealing with clients.

That covers knowing who your clients are, monitoring their activity, keeping proper records and reporting suspicious behaviour. The provider supplies tools and data. You decide how to use them and you answer for the results.
It’s worth making this clear in your own planning from day one. metatrader grey label compliance is about your processes as much as your technology.
What KYC Actually Involves

Know Your Customer is the process of confirming who your clients are before and during your relationship with them. Requirements vary by jurisdiction, but most forex broker kyc processes include a few core pieces.
Identity Verification

Clients usually provide a government-issued photo ID, such as a passport, national ID card or driving licence. Many brokers add a selfie or liveness check to make sure the person uploading the document is the person on it.
Proof of Address
A recent utility bill, bank statement or official letter showing the client’s name and address. Most regulators expect this document to be no more than a few months old.
Appropriateness or Suitability Checks

Many regulators require you to assess whether trading leveraged products suits a client. This usually means a short questionnaire on trading experience, financial knowledge and sometimes income and savings. Clients who lack experience may get warnings, lower leverage, or in some cases be declined.
Source of Funds and Wealth
For larger deposits, or clients flagged as higher risk, you may need to understand where their money comes from. That could mean payslips, tax returns, business records or other supporting documents.
AML: Keeping Watch After Onboarding
KYC confirms who someone is when they join. Anti-money laundering work continues for as long as they’re a client.
Your AML programme should cover:
Screening clients against sanctions lists and politically exposed person databases
Monitoring deposits and withdrawals for unusual patterns
Checking that withdrawals go back to the same source the funds came from where possible
Watching for third-party payments, where someone else funds a client’s account
Reporting suspicious activity to the relevant authorities

Common warning signs include large deposits followed by little or no trading and a quick withdrawal, frequent changes in payment methods, accounts linked to the same device or IP address, and clients who resist providing documents.
Risk-Based Approach
Not every client needs the same level of checks. Most regulators expect a risk-based approach, where you apply more scrutiny to higher-risk clients and keep things simpler for lower-risk ones.
Factors that often raise a client’s risk level include:
Living in, or sending funds from, higher-risk countries
Being a politically exposed person or closely linked to one
Very large or unusual deposit amounts
Complex ownership structures for corporate accounts
Write your risk categories down, apply them consistently and review them regularly. Regulators care a lot about whether your process is documented and actually followed.
Record Keeping

You’ll need to keep KYC documents, transaction records and communication logs for a set number of years, often five or more, depending on your jurisdiction. Records need to be secure, organised and quick to retrieve if a regulator or auditor asks.

This is one area where a grey label really helps. Your trading data sits on your own dedicated server instead of a shared one, which makes it simpler to pull complete, accurate records for your own clients.
How Technology Supports Compliance
Good tools won’t make you compliant on their own, but they make the work far more manageable.
CRM and Client Portal

Your CRM should handle document uploads, track verification status and store everything in one place with a clear audit trail. Clients should be able to see what’s still needed, and your team should be able to approve or reject documents with notes explaining why.
Automated Verification

Third-party ID verification services can check documents, compare selfies and screen against sanctions lists in seconds. They clear straightforward cases quickly and pass unclear ones to your compliance team.
Trading and Transaction Monitoring

Because you have admin access to your grey label server, you can set up monitoring that looks at actual trading behaviour. That might flag accounts depositing large sums without trading, linked accounts making opposite trades, or patterns that suggest abuse of bonuses or IB programmes.
Regulatory Reporting

Many regulators expect periodic reports on client funds, trading activity or capital. Back office tools that pull data directly from your MetaTrader server save hours of manual work and reduce the risk of mistakes.
Common Compliance Mistakes
A few problems come up again and again with new brokerages:
Letting clients trade before verification is complete, to avoid losing sign-ups
Accepting low-quality documents because checking takes time
Inconsistent decisions, where similar clients are treated differently
Missing withdrawal checks, especially for third-party payment methods
Policies that exist on paper but aren’t actually followed day to day
Each of these can lead to fines, lost banking relationships or worse. Payment processors are often stricter than regulators, and losing one can freeze your business overnight.
Balancing Compliance and Client Experience
Strict compliance doesn’t have to mean a frustrating sign-up. The best brokers make it feel smooth:
Explain clearly why each document is needed
Allow uploads from mobile in a few taps
Use automated checks to approve simple cases quickly
Keep clients updated on their status instead of leaving them waiting
Ask for extra documents only when there’s a real reason
Clients will accept checks they understand. What drives them away is confusion and silence.
Conclusion

Solid forex broker kyc and AML processes protect your license, your banking partners and your reputation. A grey label gives you the server control and data access to support those processes properly, but the policies, decisions and accountability stay with you. Work with a compliance specialist familiar with your jurisdiction, and build your systems around their advice.

doc-49.title: Copy Trading and Social Trading for MetaTrader Grey Label Brokers

blocks.text: Copy Trading and Social Trading for MetaTrader Grey Label Brokers

A lot of people are curious about trading but have no intention of learning chart patterns or sitting in front of a screen during the London open. They have money, interest and a phone. What they don’t have is time or confidence.

Copy trading speaks directly to them. It lets clients follow experienced traders automatically, and it gives those experienced traders a way to earn from their skill. For brokers, it opens the door to an audience that would never sign up for a standard trading account.
If you run a MetaTrader grey label, you’re well placed to offer it properly. Here’s how it works and what to think about before you launch.
Copy Trading vs Social Trading
The two terms get used interchangeably, but there’s a small difference worth knowing.
Copy trading is the mechanism. A follower links their account to a strategy provider, and trades are copied automatically in proportion to the follower’s balance and chosen settings.
Social trading is the wider experience around it. Leaderboards, trader profiles, performance stats, comments, ratings and community features that help followers decide who to trust.
Most modern platforms combine both. The copying engine does the work, and the social layer helps clients choose.
Why It Matters for Your Brokerage
Becoming a copy trading broker brings several practical benefits:
A wider audience. You reach passive investors as well as active traders.
More trading volume. One successful strategy provider can generate trades across hundreds of follower accounts.
Better retention. Followers who see steady results tend to stay longer and add funds.
A new kind of partner. Strong strategy providers bring their own audiences, much like introducing brokers.
Something to market. Leaderboards and success stories give you real content to promote.
It isn’t right for every brokerage, but for many it becomes one of the main reasons clients choose them over competitors.
Why Grey Label Makes a Difference
Copy trading systems sit closely alongside your MetaTrader server. They need to read trades from strategy accounts and place matching trades on follower accounts almost instantly.

On a white label, whether you can offer copy trading, and which system you can use, is usually up to the host. With a grey label, you have admin access to your own server, so you choose the copy trading solution, configure it the way you want, and connect it to your CRM and client portal.

That control shows up in the details. A good metatrader grey label copy trading setup lets you decide which groups can provide or follow strategies, how fees are calculated, how quickly trades are copied, and what risk limits apply.
Key Features to Look For
Flexible Copying Options

Followers should be able to choose how they copy. Common settings include copying in proportion to balance, using a fixed lot size, or applying a multiplier. They should also be able to set limits, such as a maximum drawdown that automatically stops copying.
Clear Performance Data

Followers make decisions based on what they can see. Strategy profiles should show returns over different periods, maximum drawdown, average trade length, instruments traded, number of followers and how long the strategy has been running. The more honest and complete the data, the better the decisions, and the fewer complaints later.
Fee Structures for Strategy Providers
Strategy providers need a reason to share their trades. Typical options include:
Performance fees, a share of the profits generated for followers
Subscription fees, a fixed monthly charge
Volume-based rewards, a rebate per lot traded by followers
Management fees, a small percentage of the funds following them
Your system should calculate and pay these automatically, with clear statements for both providers and followers.
Fast, Reliable Copying

Speed matters. If a follower’s trade opens several seconds after the provider’s, the results can differ noticeably, especially in fast markets. Ask any copy trading vendor how they handle latency, partial fills and slippage between master and follower accounts.
Mobile Access
Many followers will manage everything from their phones. They should be able to browse strategies, start or stop copying and check results without needing a desktop.
Risks You Need to Manage
Copy trading brings real benefits, but also real risks. Handle them carefully.
Reckless Strategy Providers

Some providers chase short-term returns with very high risk. A strategy can look brilliant for three months and then wipe out followers in an afternoon. Consider minimum track record requirements, risk scores on profiles, and caps on leverage or drawdown for strategies shown on public leaderboards.
Misleading Performance Claims

Followers need to understand that past results don’t guarantee future ones. Display risk warnings clearly, show drawdown as prominently as returns, and avoid marketing that implies guaranteed profits.
Regulatory Considerations

In some jurisdictions, offering copy trading can be viewed as portfolio management or investment advice, which may require extra permissions. Check with your compliance adviser before launch. The rules differ widely from one regulator to another.
Execution and Risk on Your Side

When one provider has hundreds of followers, a single trade can turn into a large combined position on your book. Your risk tools and liquidity setup need to handle that. Many brokers route copy trading flow differently from regular retail flow for exactly this reason.
Getting Strategy Providers on Board
A copy trading platform is only as good as the strategies on it. A few ways to attract solid providers:
Reach out to experienced traders already on your platform with consistent results
Partner with trading educators and signal providers who already have followers
Offer fair, transparent fee structures and pay on time
Give top providers visibility through featured profiles and marketing support
Set quality standards so good providers aren’t lost in a crowd of reckless ones
Some brokers also run competitions on demo or small live accounts to find promising traders early.
Launching Without Overcomplicating Things
You don’t need every feature on day one. A sensible first version might include:
A copying engine connected to your grey label server
A simple leaderboard with honest performance stats
One or two fee structures for providers
Clear risk warnings and copying limits for followers
Integration with your client portal so everything sits in one place
Add community features, advanced filters and more fee options once you see how clients actually use it.
Conclusion

Becoming a copy trading broker can bring in new clients, raise volumes and give you a strong edge in a crowded market, provided you manage risks, set fair rules and keep performance data honest. Running your own metatrader grey label copy trading setup gives you the control to do that properly.

doc-50.title: Revenue Streams of a MetaTrader Grey Label Brokerage: Spreads, Commissions and More

blocks.text: Revenue Streams of a MetaTrader Grey Label Brokerage: Spreads, Commissions and More

New brokers often build their business plan around one idea: clients trade, we take a small cut, repeat. It’s a reasonable starting point, but it misses most of what separates a brokerage that scrapes by from one that does well. The money comes in through several doors, and each one behaves differently when markets go quiet, when a big client leaves, or when a regulator changes the rules.
Running a grey label puts the controls for most of those doors in your hands. So it pays to know exactly what each one is and how to set it.
Why Control Over Pricing Changes Everything
On a white label, a lot of your pricing is shaped by the host. You might be able to tweak spreads within a range, but execution, swaps and group settings often come pre-set.

A grey label is different. With admin access to your own MetaTrader server, you decide what clients pay and how their trades are handled. That’s what makes it possible to design a revenue model around your actual clients instead of someone else’s defaults. It’s also why forex broker revenue on a grey label can look quite different from one brokerage to the next, even when they use similar technology.
The Markup on Every Price
Your liquidity provider streams you prices. You show clients slightly different ones. The gap between them is your markup, and it’s the most familiar source of income in the industry.
What many brokers overlook is how precisely this can be tuned. Rather than adding the same markup everywhere, you can:
Keep majors like EURUSD and GBPUSD sharp, since traders compare them constantly
Price exotics and less liquid instruments more generously, where clients expect wider spreads
Set different markups for beginner accounts, VIP accounts and IB-referred groups
A small change across a busy symbol adds up quickly. Equally, getting greedy on the pairs everyone watches is the fastest way to lose experienced traders.
Charging Per Trade Instead

Not every trader wants costs hidden in the spread. Scalpers, algorithmic traders and high-volume clients usually prefer raw pricing and a visible commission per lot. They can calculate exactly what each trade costs, which matters a great deal for their strategies.

Offering a commission-based account can bring in clients who would never consider a standard account. On your grey label server, you can set commissions by group, scale them down for higher volumes, or create special terms for professional clients and money managers.
Picking the Right Mix

Most brokers offer both. A standard account with no commission and slightly wider spreads works for newer or occasional traders. A raw account with commission suits the serious crowd. Running both lets you serve each group without forcing either into a model they dislike.
Overnight Positions
Clients who keep trades open past the daily rollover pay or earn swap, based on the interest rate gap between two currencies. Brokers add a margin on top of the base rate.

It’s quiet money, rarely noticed by short-term traders but steady across longer-term positions. Since you set swap rates yourself on a grey label, you can stay competitive on popular pairs while earning a fair amount elsewhere.
If you offer swap-free accounts, plan them carefully. A fixed holding fee after a certain number of days is common, but the terms need to be transparent and applied consistently.
Taking the Other Side
This is the part of brokerage income people argue about most.
When you keep a client’s trade in-house rather than passing it to the market, you become the counterparty. Their loss is your gain, and their gain is your cost. This is known as B-booking.

Many brokers combine approaches. Large, consistently profitable or fast-trading clients go to liquidity providers. Smaller, less experienced flow stays internal. Handled with discipline, this hybrid approach can be a major contributor to metatrader grey label profit.

The word “discipline” is doing a lot of work there. Without proper risk tools, clear routing rules and someone watching exposure in real time, B-book revenue can turn negative very quickly. A grey label gives you the access to set all of this up yourself, but it doesn’t remove the risk.
Income From Copy Trading and Managed Money
Copy trading, PAMM and MAM accounts add another layer. You can earn a share of performance or subscription fees charged by strategy providers and money managers.

The bigger effect, though, is volume. A single trader with a few hundred followers turns one decision into hundreds of trades. Each of those carries spread, commission or swap revenue, which can make a well-run copy trading platform one of the more valuable parts of the business.
Smaller Streams That Still Count
Beyond trading, a few extras can help:
VPS hosting for clients running EAs around the clock
Paid education, mentoring or premium webinars
Signal services and advanced analytics tools
New instruments such as share CFDs, commodities or crypto, where permitted
Individually they’re modest. Together, they can noticeably improve your margins and make your offering feel more complete.
Fees: Use Sparingly

Inactivity fees, withdrawal charges and conversion fees can bring in some revenue, but they come at a cost to trust. Traders are quick to share stories of brokers who nickel-and-dime them. Many brokers now treat zero-fee deposits and withdrawals as part of their marketing and earn their money through trading instead. If you do charge anything, keep it modest and spell it out clearly.
Where the Money Goes Out
Revenue isn’t profit. Before you can judge whether your model works, account for what flows the other way:
Grey label, bridge, CRM and other technology fees
Liquidity and execution costs
Payment processor fees and rolling reserves
IB rebates and affiliate payouts
Salaries, compliance, audits and office costs
Marketing and acquisition spend
B-book losses during periods when clients do well
IB rebates often surprise new brokers. Generous payouts can absorb most of the spread revenue from referred clients, so set rebate levels with your margins in mind, not just to win partners.
Don’t Lean on One Stream
Brokerages that rely heavily on a single source of income are fragile. A regulator restricting leverage, a key IB leaving, or a long stretch of calm markets can hit hard.

The more resilient approach spreads income across markups, commissions, swaps, carefully managed internal flow, copy trading volume and a few value-added services. When one slows, the others keep the lights on.
Conclusion

Steady forex broker revenue doesn’t come from squeezing clients. It comes from pricing each product thoughtfully, managing risk properly and building several income sources that support each other. A grey label gives you direct access to every one of those levers, and that’s where real metatrader grey label profit starts.
